#4339. 7 Unique JRPG Mechanics We Want in Modern Releases

Murillo Zerbinatto is a JRPG enthusiast, writer, and editor. He has played over 300 RPGs during his gaming career, with 90% of them being JRPGs.

JRPGs are evolving in a fairly consistent way. While modern titles keep several staples of the genre, such as a fixed story, a focus on character development, innovation in the battle system, and some wacky progression systems, sometimes it feels like they leave behind certain mechanics that could be put to great use today. Many JRPGs of yesteryear featured unique mechanics that were either never re-explored, or, if they were, remained confined to indie games and flew under the radar of many players.

From twists on classic turn-based combat to card systems and more, these JRPGs all have very unique battle mechanics.

Today, I want to explore some JRPG mechanics I would love to see in modern releases. Most are battle-related, though a few, if properly implemented, could expand exploration and even improve how the game's systems interact. That is not to say they have never appeared in other games throughout the years, but I would love to see them become much more mainstream.

When I first played Vagrant Story, I barely knew what I was doing. When chaining attacks, you can aim at enemies' limbs, yet all I ever did was try to go straight for the head or body to defeat the foe as fast as possible. How naive I was, because against bosses, that mindless strategy never paid off, especially if I was not wielding an appropriate weapon.

This mechanic of targeting different body parts has popped up in other JRPGs, though usually you can only hit distinct areas when an enemy is preparing a specific attack. I would love to see a JRPG reuse this mechanic exhaustively, letting players willingly target different enemy limbs and trigger distinct tactical outcomes.

One of Star Ocean's greatest strengths is its Item Creation system. To me, gaining levels wasn't about learning new combat skills, but it was all about earning points to invest in Customization and unlock new crafting potential, whether forging an endgame weapon at the start of the game or diving into other side activities. Still, the most entertaining feature, even at the cost of my relationship with my party members, was Pickpocketing.

Leveling up your Pickpocketing skill lets you steal from every NPC in town and score the wildest variety of items. The sheer thrill of not knowing what you would get, whether a simple consumable or an insanely overpowered piece of gear, was endlessly fun and had me making the rounds through town as if I were living inside GTA. As mentioned, doing so affects how your party members perceive the protagonist, so if you are aiming for a specific ending, watch out for the consequences of your actions.

This entry is less about battle mechanics and more about dungeon delving. As much as I love modern JRPGs, especially for their evolution in combat gameplay, narrative, and character development, I feel some are still a bit lacking in the level design department. Too many dungeons are simply streamlined corridors, featuring an occasional puzzle that solves itself before you even begin thinking through the solution.

Plenty of classic JRPGs boasted incredible level design, but if I had to highlight just one, it would be Wild Arms. This series blended the interactive tools of action-adventure games and let the scope of exploration expand incrementally. Moreover, acquiring new tools encouraged backtracking and re-exploring older dungeons, much like a Metroidvania, to hunt down hidden treasures.

I never had much contact with Sega consoles growing up, which led me to neglect their JRPG catalog for quite a while. I played Phantasy Star IV fairly recently, and during my playthrough, a friend told me to set up Macros using specific skills while emphasizing that the execution order mattered. So I complied, and when I stepped into battle, oh boy, what a beautiful surprise.

The Sega Genesis wasn't your first choice for JRPGs back in the day, but it had a surprisingly large selection of them when all was said and done.

For those who don't know, depending on the sequence in which you cast spells and skills, they fuse together to unleash an entirely new combo attack. It is a deeply entertaining combo system that later surfaced in future JRPGs like Breath of Fire IV. It feels distinct from two characters simply chaining standard turns together, because there is a real sense of mystique in discovering the combinations, and I will confess that without a GameFAQs guide, I never would have figured them all out. Still, it is pretty amazing and elevated turn-based combat to new heights.

Staying on the topic of skill combos, Chrono Trigger pulled off something similar yet distinctly its own. If two or three party members mastered specific techniques and had their ATB gauges filled simultaneously, they could execute a Double or Triple Tech, each carrying a unique effect. The very first time I discovered this, as I imagine most players did, was with Crono and Lucca's Fire Whirl. A whole new world of tactical possibilities opened up in that exact moment.

Chrono Trigger pushed the concept even further, and just when I expected the game to stick to Double Techs, the JRPG introduced Triple Techs. I don't know about you, but I built my entire party around these Techs, and luckily, nearly every character paired well with the rest of the roster. Triple Techs were slightly more restrictive, yet they still allowed for remarkably efficient setups, especially when hunting for Techs capable of healing the entire party at once.

Breath of Fire is my favorite JRPG series, and within it, Breath of Fire III stands as my absolute favorite entry. Whenever people ask me why, a massive part of my reasoning rests on its Gene splicing system, a feature Breath of Fire IV dropped for reasons I still don't understand, which was a real shame. I loved transforming into dozens of distinct dragons, even if Ryu and Fou-Lu's half-dragon forms looked awesome in their own right.

Essentially, you discovered Dragon Genes scattered across the world and could combine up to three at once to transform Ryu into wildly different dragon forms, each boasting unique strengths and abilities. The thing is, I don't necessarily need the exact Gene system back, but I would love a transformation-focused JRPG where characters can shift forms mid-battle and completely alter the flow of combat. Even better if those transformations feature distinct variations that actively reward exploration.

I know there are many, many caveats surrounding the progression mechanics of Final Fantasy VIII, though I feel the bulk of player complaints stems from the Draw system rather than the Junction system itself. There is a historical reason behind that, as Hiroyuki Ito, creator of both the ATB and Junction systems, left the Final Fantasy VIII team before finalizing the battle mechanics to direct Final Fantasy IX, leaving his original vision somewhat incomplete.

Just imagine what it could have been if fully realized. The Junction system is remarkably dynamic. Beyond simply slotting spells to boost each character's raw stats, you could attach status ailments to basic physical attacks, build elemental resistances, tailor one character toward magic and agility while turning another into a pure strength powerhouse, and so on. Pair that flexibility with specialized commands learned through Guardian Forces, and what appears on the surface to be standard turn-based combat suddenly gains deep strategic layers.

From Chained Echoes to Octopath Traveler II, these JRPGs on the Switch are more about exploring the overworld than mindlessly grinding levels.

#4338. For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard

How often you exercise may matter more for your mental health than how hard you push yourself during a workout. A large study of Norwegian college students found that those who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety one year later. The findings suggest that maintaining a consistent exercise routine could be particularly important for supporting mental well-being.

The research, published in the open access journal PLOS One, was conducted by Michael Grasdalsmoen of Western Norway University of Applied Sciences and his colleagues. Their results point to the potential benefits of exercising regularly rather than focusing primarily on longer or more demanding workouts.

Why Exercise Habits Matter for Mental Health

Depression, anxiety, and other common mental health conditions are among the leading causes of disability in young adults worldwide. The college years can be an especially challenging period as students adjust to new academic, social, and personal responsibilities. Identifying everyday behaviors that may help protect mental health is therefore an important research priority.

Although previous research has linked regular physical activity to better psychological well-being, many young adults remain physically inactive. Scientists have also had relatively limited evidence about how exercise habits relate to the development of mental health conditions over time, particularly when those conditions are evaluated using standardized diagnostic tools.

To investigate this relationship, Grasdalsmoen and his team followed 10,460 full-time students enrolled in higher education in Norway. Participants ranged in age from 18 to 35.

At the beginning of the study, students completed questionnaires describing their exercise habits, including how frequently they worked out, how strenuous their activities were, how long they exercised, and how many total hours they were active each week. One year later, they completed a self-administered diagnostic assessment designed to identify common mental health disorders.

Exercise Frequency May Matter More Than Intensity

The researchers found that students who reported lower levels of physical activity were more likely to meet diagnostic criteria for anxiety or depression one year later. However, not every aspect of exercise showed the same relationship with mental health.

Exercise frequency emerged as a particularly consistent factor. How often students exercised was more reliably associated with their later mental health than the intensity of their workouts or the amount of time they spent exercising.

The researchers also identified differences between men and women. Among women, lower exercise intensity was associated with a greater likelihood of anxiety and depression. Among men, spending fewer total hours exercising each week showed a stronger association with these conditions.

Overall, the likelihood of common mental health disorders decreased as weekly exercise increased, with this pattern continuing up to approximately 10 hours of physical activity per week.

The results also support the World Health Organization's recommendation that adults complete at least 150 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity each week.

Regular Exercise Could Help Support Student Mental Health

Taken together, the findings suggest that exercising consistently may be especially valuable for reducing the likelihood of anxiety and depression among college students. Rather than concentrating exclusively on workout intensity or duration, maintaining a regular routine could be an important part of supporting mental health.

However, the researchers emphasize that their observational study cannot establish a direct cause-and-effect relationship. Although students who exercised more regularly tended to have better mental health outcomes, the results do not prove that exercise itself prevented depression or anxiety.

Even with this limitation, promoting accessible opportunities for physical activity could be a useful part of broader efforts to improve student well-being. Such efforts may be especially relevant for students who are beginning to experience mental health difficulties or symptoms that have not yet reached the threshold for a clinical diagnosis.

The authors add: "Our findings show that students who engage in regular physical exercise are at lower risk of developing common mental disorders over time. These findings highlight the importance of making physical activity an accessible and natural part of student life."

"Mental health among students is a growing public health concern. Our findings suggest that supporting students to be physically active may contribute to better mental health and should be recognized as an important part of a healthy learning environment."

Funding: The SHoT study was financially supported by the Norwegian Ministry of Education and Research (2017) and the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services (2016). Neither funding organization participated in designing the research, collecting or analyzing data, deciding whether to publish the findings, or preparing the manuscript.

Materials provided by PLOS. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4337. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4335. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

#4334. Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months

A ketogenic diet may offer significant health benefits beyond weight loss, according to a new clinical trial that compared three popular approaches to eating. Researchers found that people following a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat diet experienced substantially greater reductions in liver fat than those eating Mediterranean or low-fat diets, even though all three groups lost similar amounts of weight.

The results were especially striking for people with prediabetes. After just four to five months on a ketogenic (or "Keto") diet, approximately half of the participants no longer met the diagnostic criteria for the condition. The findings, published in the journal Cell Metabolism, suggest that the types of foods people eat can influence metabolic health in ways that extend beyond the number of pounds they lose.

"We know weight loss can improve metabolic health in people who are obese," says Samuel Klein, the study's corresponding author at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, Missouri. "Our data suggest that if you have high liver fat content and prediabetes, reducing carbohydrate intake can have important therapeutic effects on metabolism beyond just weight loss alone."

Comparing Keto, Mediterranean, and Low-Fat Diets

An estimated 40% of American adults have obesity, a condition associated with increased risks of type 2 diabetes, fatty liver disease, and other health problems. Doctors frequently recommend dietary changes to help patients lose weight and improve their metabolic health, which refers to how effectively the body manages energy, blood sugar, and fats.

Three commonly recommended approaches are low-carbohydrate diets, low-fat diets, and Mediterranean diets. Although each can support weight loss, researchers have been uncertain whether one offers additional metabolic advantages when the amount of weight lost is roughly the same.

These eating patterns differ substantially in their nutritional makeup. Low-carbohydrate approaches, including Atkins and ketogenic diets, restrict carbohydrate consumption, while low-fat diets may obtain as much as 70% of their calories from carbohydrates. The Mediterranean diet emphasizes plant foods such as vegetables, nuts, and olive oil, along with moderate amounts of fish and dairy. Ketogenic diets, meanwhile, can include considerable amounts of fat from animal products, including saturated fat.

To compare their effects, Klein and his colleagues recruited 42 adults with obesity, prediabetes, and fatty liver disease. Prediabetes occurs when blood sugar levels rise above the normal range but have not yet reached the threshold for type 2 diabetes. Fatty liver disease involves excess fat accumulating inside liver cells, which can interfere with the body's ability to regulate metabolism.

A Controlled Clinical Trial With Similar Weight Loss

Participants were randomly assigned to follow one of three diets: ketogenic, Mediterranean, or a low-fat diet emphasizing plant-based foods. To ensure that participants followed their assigned eating plans, the research team supplied all their meals and arranged weekly consultations with a dietitian.

The diets had sharply different proportions of carbohydrates and fat. In the ketogenic group, carbohydrates accounted for just 4% of daily calories, while fat supplied 73%. The Mediterranean group received 50% of its calories from carbohydrates and 35% from fat. The plant-forward group consumed 70% of its calories from carbohydrates and 15% from fat.

Researchers adjusted calorie intake individually so that participants across all three groups lost approximately 10% of their starting body weight. Reaching this target took about four to five months.

By the end of the intervention, every group had experienced meaningful reductions in body fat and improvements in insulin sensitivity. Insulin is the hormone that helps move sugar from the bloodstream into cells, where it can be used for energy. Greater insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

However, the similarities between the groups largely ended there.

The ketogenic diet produced the largest improvements in several important indicators of liver function and metabolic health.

Participants following keto experienced an average 67% reduction in liver fat, compared with a 45% reduction in both the Mediterranean and low-fat groups. Because the groups lost comparable amounts of weight, the difference suggests that carbohydrate restriction may influence liver fat through mechanisms beyond weight loss alone.

To investigate these effects, the researchers collected blood samples repeatedly over a 24-hour period, allowing them to observe changes in hormones involved in energy metabolism.

The ketogenic group showed the greatest increase in glucagon, a hormone that helps regulate the body's energy supply and promotes the reduction of fat stored in the liver. Participants on keto also experienced the largest decrease in insulin levels, another change that can help reduce liver fat accumulation.

One result was particularly unexpected. Despite getting nearly three-quarters of their calories from fat, the keto participants did not show an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels during the study.

"The most surprising finding was that participants in the ketogenic diet group didn't experience an increase in blood fat or cholesterol levels despite consuming the most fat," says Max Petersen, the study's first author at Washington University School of Medicine.

Half of Keto Participants No Longer Had Prediabetes

The benefits extended beyond liver fat. After the weight-loss intervention, approximately 50% of participants assigned to the ketogenic diet no longer met the criteria for prediabetes. By comparison, that milestone was reached by 29% of those on the Mediterranean diet and just 7% of those following the low-fat, plant-forward diet.

These differences are notable because prediabetes signals an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes. Bringing blood sugar levels below the prediabetes threshold is an important improvement, although it does not necessarily mean the condition has been permanently reversed.

The findings also highlight a potentially important distinction in weight management: losing weight and improving metabolic health are closely connected, but they are not necessarily the same thing. The composition of a diet may affect how the body handles blood sugar, stores fat, and responds to hormones, even when weight loss is similar.

Researchers emphasize the growing importance of understanding these effects as powerful new obesity treatments become more widely available. GLP-1 medications, which act on hormone pathways involved in appetite and blood sugar regulation, have transformed the treatment of obesity by helping many patients achieve substantial weight loss.

"GLP-1-based medications have revolutionized the therapy of obesity. We now have a very effective pharmacotherapy for achieving significant weight loss," Petersen says. "But in addition, our study shows that the specific composition of the diet can give you added benefits."

Although the trial was relatively small and lasted only four to five months, its carefully controlled design offers evidence that dietary composition can play an important role in metabolic health. Longer studies involving more participants will be needed to determine whether the benefits persist and how different diets compare over time.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital.

#4333. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4332. App Army Assemble: Cult Vacui - "Should you play this eerie point-and-click adventure?"

On mobile, point-and-click adventures feel right at home. Instead of clicking with a mouse, you can tap objects, and it often feels very intuitive. As such, they're a favourite among our App Army readers. So, whenever one comes along, we like to get their thoughts. This week, we've given them the spooky Cult Vacui. Here's what they said:

I love the atmosphere you have 24 mins to complete a ritual before you. Get possessed by a demon. The atmosphere is very good, and the artwork is great. My only problem is I have fat fingers. So selection can be difficult. The idea is that certain actions can take up your time. A bit like Blue Prince, I think.

You repeat until you work out the sequence of events. To be honest, I’m not so good at point-and-clicks, but the story and atmosphere keep me hooked. Just the touch controls feel fiddly. The artwork is a nice pixel style. Very much like the classic Lucas art games.

I’m not usually good at point-and-clicks, so what really grabbed me here is the unique time-management mechanic. Every action ticks down the clock, creating tension without real-time panic. I definitely struggled at first and died a few times trying to get it right,

Thankfully, the manual save system (allowing you multiple save points) helped me go back and try different strategies. Combined with the eerie graphics and creepy atmosphere, it was much more enjoyment than frustration. It's a short (about two hours) atmospheric winner on iOS.

Cult Vacui is an old-school point-and-click adventure where you play as a man possessed by a demon and must find a way to exorcise the demon. In the first part of the game, you have a limited number of moves to get rid of the demon. This involves finding and manipulating objects to perform an exorcism ritual.

The graphics are atmospheric and pixelated and look like a PC game from the 90s. There is no hint function, and the tight number of moves can make the first part of the game frustrating. Saying that I enjoyed playing this adventure. I recommend it.

Cult Vacui is a pixel art stylised point-and-click survival horror game. Right from the start, I was pulled into CV’s handcrafted 19th-century setting. Puzzles can be difficult with no hand-holding, and every action takes time away from your 25-minute countdown, adding a real sort of tension to your playthrough.

The whole retro vibe works great too; the minimalistic colour tones of the graphics, along with its eerie soundtrack, create just the right amount of spookiness. Cult Vacui fits perfectly on mobile and deserves a spot on your device. What is the App Army? The App Army is Pocket Gamer's lovely community of mobile game experts. As often as possible, we ask them for their thoughts on the latest games and share them with you.

#4331. 10 Most Unhinged NPC Interactions in GTA 6

Aden Carter is a Contributor at DualShockers who has been covering games professionally since 2020. He specializes in lists and guides, with a focus on RPGs, horror games, survival horror, Soulslikes, cozy/sim games, and action-adventure titles. Before joining DualShockers, Aden contributed to GameRant, XDA, Gamepur, I

The Grand Theft Auto series is known for its absurdity, and it gave us some many memorable moments throughout its run. However, Grand Theft Auto 6 is taking the absurdity to a new level, with NPCs that are far more over-the-top than ever before.

Leonida is no stranger to the strange and weird, and since the first trailer for GTA 6, you could tell that it would be a place that is off the wall. There are old people running away from the cops on mobility scooters, people you can spot in… unfortunate positions, and even some strange moments that catch you completely off guard.

If you are planning on taking a trip across Leonida, whether it is by fan boat or sports car, get ready to see some strange happenings all across the state.

Shortly after you start up GTA 6, Brian will ask you to stop by a girl named Mandy’s house to collect the rent. This sounds like a fairly simple job, and there shouldn’t be anything that you have to worry about with it.

Of course, nothing is ever simple in GTA, and you have to put up with a girl who desperately needs a tall glass of Jason. She is perhaps the thirstiest character I have ever seen, and she consistently tries to lure Jason into a compromising position.

She goes so far as to catch Jason off guard by wearing next to nothing while he tries to fix her sink. Plus, you find out she clogged the sink herself to get Jason to come over. She has issues.

One of the many side characters in GTA 6 is Cal. He is Jason’s friend, and he is also one of the most absurd characters you will run into throughout the game. He constantly has something to say, and it is often hilarious.

During one of the nights early on in the game, Cal comes over and installs a JoyStation for Jason. The two of them rearrange the house, and then they have a few drinks while they chat through the night.

It ends with things getting a bit wild and the pair end up spooning in the bedroom. You awaken to a strange sight, and it fits Cal’s character perfectly.

Jason and Lucia are played by Dylan Rourke and Manni L. Perez, respectively.

It is normal for NPCs to get angry at you while you are driving in a Grand Theft Auto game. After all, you probably don’t drive very well and have little regard for the rules of the road. Well, the NPCs in GTA 6 take things to a new level.

Sometimes, when you bump into a vehicle while driving around Leonida, the NPC will get so angry that they chase you down. This can go on for a while, and the result is often the NPC plowing into your vehicle to stop you.

After this, they get out and assault you for hitting their car. It is a much bigger reaction than NPCs had in GTA 5 and it is something that fits in the land of Leonida.

Bert is a strange character who is obviously meant to signify the less reasonable members of the right-wing political ideology. He appears next to Mandy’s house with his pants down, flashing his genitalia to Mandy’s neighbors while screaming at them.

It is a strange sight to behold, but what is even more strange is that the landlord shows up to fight Bert. The man gets out of his truck, starts yelling at Bert, and tells him to get off his property.

However, things take a turn when they realize that they see eye-to-eye, with both of them wearing shirts of a similar fashion. Bert then gets offered a job while his family jewels are blowing in the wind.

There are plenty of random events that can happen in GTA 6, especially when you are exploring Vice City. Some of the NPCs around here get a little bit crazy. One such way is through their driving.

One of the game’s random events involves a car that comes careening down the highway only to take a sharp turn, flip, and get destroyed. It is a wild turn of events that you can get involved in.

If you stop to see if everyone is okay, the NPCs involved will freak out about the crash and high tail it out of there before the cops come. This leaves you with a bag of drugs that you can take to a stash house. Pretty convenient.

During one of the main story missions, Jason and Lucia have a night on the town, which leads them to a fun time in Vice City with Mattia. The night culminates in a massive party in a hotel room. During this party, however, Lucia gets separated from Jason.

While separated from Jason, you get to wander into various hotel rooms, and some of them are not for the faint of heart. For instance, one room has you walking in on a man dressed head to toe in leather, with a woman who is …inserting something into his body that is usually exit only.

It is a very unexpected scene that will catch you entirely off guard, and it is also one of the most unhinged things I have seen in a game between two consenting NPCs.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a nominee for Game of the Year. It was selected at the last minute, but there are plenty of reasons it deserves the award.

There are some NPCs who are into doing some wild stuff in Leonida, and I am not just talking about wild in the bedroom like the NPC from earlier. Instead, I am talking about some extreme stunts. This one might also count as an easter egg, but it is an interesting interaction.

At the top of a radio tower, which just so happens to be one of the tallest spots in the game, you can find an influencer who is climbing the tower. She can be found hanging off of it, and if you interact with her, you will question why she is doing it.

She will respond by telling you that she climbed the tower because another influencer named Kelly Explores did it. Either way, it is weird and makes the list.

There are some pretty desperate NPCs in Grand Theft Auto 6. Some of them are willing to go to great lengths to make some money and get ahead in life. One guy in particular is willing to risk it all by robbing a store, but his weapon of choice isn’t a pistol, shotgun, or assault rifle.

Instead, it is a banana. That’s right, a banana. You can happen to walk into a store and see a man threatening the clerk, but while the store clerk can’t see the man’s weapon, you can clearly see that he is holding a banana behind his back.

You can put a stop to the man by threatening him, or you can watch the scene play out. Either way, it is pretty hilarious and pretty unhinged of him to attempt a robbery with produce as a weapon.

It is hilarious the type of people who think they can get away with something in GTA 6. For instance, there are some elderly folks who think that they can just rob people on a mobility scooter.

There are a few outcomes that this can have, but it all starts with a woman with a mullet driving around on a mobility scooter. She will pull a gun on someone, who will end up giving her their money.

She will then pull a gun on you, and you can choose to give her the money, wait for the cops to arrive, and see her get arrested, or you can decline. If you decline, she will curse at you and drive away. Better yet, you can just push her over and take her money.

There’s a chance that you will run into some NPCs in the Grassrivers who got their van stuck in the mud. This kind of thing happens to everyone, and so you may be inclined to help them out. After all, they will actually ask for your assistance.

If you help them out, they will reward you with some drugs and be on their way. Nothing too special, unless you end up looking in the back of the van, in which case, things get wild.

If you walk up to the back of the van, one of the men will tell you to stop, but it is too late. Inside, is a tiger, and opening the doors will cause it to jump out and pounce on one of the NPCs, taking his face clean off.

Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers an enormous open world, a gripping story, a vibrant Vice City and an astonishing range of activities.

#4329. Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.

Co-author Beizhan Yan of Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory emphasized that microplastics can originate from numerous sources, including plastic manufacturing facilities and laundromats. Everyday processes, such as heating materials in a microwave or leaving bottled water exposed to sunlight during storage, can also contribute to the formation of tiny plastic particles.

"This work has significant implications for environmental and human health," said co-author Beizhan Yan of Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "In certain environments, such as discharges from plastic manufacturers and laundromats, microplastics can form and enter aquatic environments. This work also indicates that radicals can form on hydrophobic plastic surfaces in water, which could affect ecosystems and human health following exposure. In addition, various uses and processes in our daily lives can generate microplastics, including microwave heating, sunlight exposure of bottled water during storage. This foundational work provides a potential pathway for understanding their health impacts."

By revealing that microplastics can actively alter the chemistry of surrounding water, the research adds a new dimension to concerns about plastic pollution. It also establishes a potential mechanism for investigating how these widespread particles interact with living systems, while opening the door to strategies for reducing their environmental and health risks.

#4326. Deltarune Chapter 6 'Structurally Complete,' Chapter 7 Development Underway

Daniel is a lifelong gamer with a love for various genres and gameplay styles who enjoys exploring games and playing from various angles.

Chapter 5 of Toby Fox’s newest indie game opus, Deltarune, launched back in June of this year. It’s kind of interesting to think about; when that chapter launched, it completely dominated the gaming sphere for a good month, even if it didn’t quite hit with everyone. Now that GTA 6 is out and completely taken over the scene, it’s gone largely quiet outside of its specific fanbase. Still, perhaps that’s for the best. A little less attention means that Fox and his team will have some extra breathing room as they work on the next stretch of the game, which is set to encompass both Chapter 6 and Chapter 7.

Based on some little hints that Fox has previously dropped, Chapter 6 will be when the game starts reaching its narrative crux, bringing an end to “wacky silly adventures” in the face of all the mysteries that have been building up, and there are a lot of them. It’s still going to be a while before we actually get to see any of this, mind you, but according to Fox, development is going pretty swimmingly.

In the newest edition of the Deltarune newsletter for Fall 2026, Fox announced that Chapter 6 is “structurally complete,” in that you can technically play it from start to finish. The next orders of business will be to hammer out the nitty-gritty details, as well as get things rolling in earnest on Chapter 7.

In both the world and the characters, there are Deltarune Details That Make the World Feel Stranger Every Time You Replay It.

As Fox explained in the newsletter, Chapter 6 is a “structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end. All the maps, events, and battles exist,” though he parenthetically noted that there’s a particular optional event that’s causing the overall development to drag out a bit.

“By the time you read this, we should have started the localization and some preliminary testing. Much of the game looks complete… but, some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation, so it's going to take a bit longer before we can really move to full-on testing,” Fox said.

He admitted that, while Chapter 6 will be shorter in length than the previous chapters, it’s going to be a pivotal one, and he wants it to hit as hard as it possibly can. In short, this is not a process that can be rushed; it’ll only be ready once he’s satisfied with it.

By the time you read this, we should have started the localization and some preliminary testing.

On the bright side, thanks to a fan vote, Fox opted to share a brief sneak peek of Chapter 6 in the form of a quote unquote “stupid scene” involving Queen meeting with Pink in Castle Town and being… her Queenly self, let’s say. Hey, it made me laugh.

The newsletter also shared an update on Chapter 7, though as Fox rather succinctly puts it, “Well, we've only just started…”

While development on Chapter 7 has only just begun, Fox feels as though he’s on the right track with his team and their work. Apparently, the way they’re handling development is by having Fox read out the events and dialogue of the chapter to the team, then stopping just as the story reaches a critical point. The only way for the team to find out what happens next is for more of the game to be completed. A bit of an unusual approach, but apparently, “Everyone agrees it's more fun this way.”

With so much of Deltarune already under the team’s belt, Fox is feeling optimistic as they all get started in earnest on Chapter 7. “Unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence...!”

Fox concluded the newsletter with a reminder that, as development on the game goes on, the dev team keeps getting bigger, which is why more time is needed to ensure everything comes out right.

“I know it's probably annoying to not have any updates, but no news is good news.”

#4325. Leingham Tavern Story has you turning dungeon crawling into a restaurant business

Alan gets stronger by eating his own cooking

In an RPG, you’d expect to become stronger by hitting things, but in Kemco’s latest, you do it by eating your own cooking (abs are made in the kitchen, as the saying goes). Leingham Tavern Story: Alan and the Time Goddess is out now on the App Store and Google Play. It’s a dungeon crawler and a restaurant sim at the same time, and there’s an orphanage to save on top.

That orphanage is the whole reason you’re doing any of this. It’s about to close down, and Alan and his mates reckon a busy tavern will make enough money to keep it going. Which means heading down into dungeons for ingredients.

You can go back to these every day, picking things up from gathering points and getting into turn-based fights with whatever monsters are lurking about. You’ll want better gear for the fights and you’ll want levels too, but like I said, you get most of those from eating when you’re back.

Back at the tavern, you can buy recipes, and you can also mix ingredients yourself and see what you get. There are more than 800 dishes to find. There’s a field out the back for growing vegetables too, plus a fishing spot for when you fancy a break (apparently you can catch something you weren’t expecting, though I’ve no idea what).

Then there’s running the place, which is what actually keeps the orphanage going. Once a few dishes are on the menu, you open the doors, and from there it’s a case of changing what you cook to suit the season and whatever customers are into at the time, and working out which of your staff should be doing what. Leingham Tavern Story only comes in English and Japanese, and there’s no controller support either.

#4320. How to Play GTA 6 in First Person, Until Rockstar Patches It

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

GTA 6 had a stellar launch, with two million XBOX players swarming to New Zealand to start their playthrough as early as possible, boasting eye-watering sales figures, and breaking viewership records.

Bugs and glitches are just a part of modern gaming. Some can be game-breaking, others produce some funny moments, and some can actually be useful. One GTA 6 glitch that is gathering a lot of attention is one that lets players access a first-person mode.

'Weird Al' Yankovic confirms he's a GTA 6 Vice City FM DJ and reveals his other roles, including writing commercials and voicing Burger Shot ads.

As expected, GTA 6 is played in third-person and although many players appreciate a first-person mode, it is absent at launch, or at least, officially.

There is a glitch that enables a first-person look. It can be a little fiddly at first, but once you get the hang of it, you will have a better view at the sights. We have all the details you need to know about how to enter first-person mode the next time you load up the game.

YouTuber OneBoyler posted a video demonstrating how to do the GTA 6 first-person glitch on PlayStation. To perform the glitch, pause the game and go to the in-game settings, under the Controller tab, scroll down until you see Touch Pad Button. Change the Touch Pad Button to Camera 2. This setting changes your touchpad from opening the map to altering your camera view.

Next, sit in the driver’s seat of a vehicle and take out your mobile phone by pressing up on the D-Pad. Put your phone away by hitting circle on a PlayStation controller and then instantly spam your touchpad button.

Once successful, you will see the world from your character’s perspective, holding the wheel of the car. From this point onward, you can safely exit the car with first-person view intact and even access your loadout. Equipping a gun allows you to hold it realistically, and the animations are compatible with first-person mode.

Bugs and glitches are just a part of modern gaming. Some can be game-breaking, others produce some funny moments, and some can actually be useful.

Also, you can drive in first-person, bringing a new level of immersion to the already gorgeous and detailed world around you. The city lights reflecting off the front of your car hit different when you’re cruising around the streets.

It’s worth noting that to return to third-person mode, you must reload your save. Make sure you save at the right time and don’t make any progress you want to risk losing while experimenting with the first-person view.

When GTA 5 launched on XBOX 360 and PlayStation 3 back in 2013, a first-person mode was absent. Only when GTA 5 was ported to XBOX One, PlayStation 4, and PC did a first-person perspective arrive in the game. Included were an optional first-person cover system, a new targeting system, traditional FPS controls, and fresh animations that allowed players to see the world in a whole new way.

If history were to repeat itself, a first-person mode could be on the cards for GTA 6 in a future update. For now, if you want to explore Leonida in first-person, you’ll have to do so using the glitch.

It’s unknown what the first post-launch GTA 6 patch will entail, but if it doesn’t bring a first-person mode with it, players will be hoping that Rockstar Games decides against patching out this particular bug.

Grand Theft Auto 6 is full of lively NPCs who get very unhinged at times, but these NPCs take things a bit over the top.
